newsitem.title: USA: Hormats sees no major drop in Japan US debt buying.
newsitem.headline: Hormats sees no major drop in Japan US debt buying.

text.p: Robert Hormats, vice chairman at Goldman Sachs International, said Wednesday that recent U.S. current account numbers suggest there could be a tapering off of Japanese purchases of U.S. Treasuries, but said he does not expect any major pullback.

"It doesn't mean a wholesale pullback, it doesn't mean they're going to stop buying. It just means that the risk in the back of their minds goes up the longer these very large trade imbalances continue," said Hormats, speaking in an exclusive interview with Reuters Financial Television.

The 'Heard on the Street' column of Wednesday's Wall Street Journal quoted Hormats as saying, "This is a big issue going forward. I think Japanese institutions will slow their purchases (of U.S. Treasuries), which could begin to push up interest rates."
Speaking to Reuters, Hormats appeared to play down the remarks, which had weighed on Treasuries and the dollar early on Wednesday.

"My comment (in the Journal) was really related specifically to growing concern about the trade and current account imbalance which would add to the risk factor for institutional investors who are contemplating buying dollar assets," Hormats told RFTV.
"It doesn't mean there's going to be an enormous sea-change in Japanese investor thinking...," he added.
Hormats also said he believes the U.S. stock and bond markets will continue to demonstrate resiliency.
"These markets have been able to pull back a little bit and then bounce back and I don't think we're going to see anything very different from that in this current environment," said Hormats.

"In the medium-term I'm still quite optimistic about the U.S. equity market," Hormats said. "I don't think this rally is necessarily over, but if there's an interest rate correction, it could lead to a slight correction in the market.
